title: Part 3
text: hundred. Classrooms had multiplied, doors appearing in walls that hadn't had them before, the whole structure spreading outward and inward simultaneously like something organic. The Entity had renovated thoroughly and without apology, and the result was something that had stopped pretending to make sense. Shadows clung too tight in the corners. The walls didn’t meet right. The beam from the flashlight couldn’t quite seem to settle anywhere useful, making everything feel ever so slightly like a fever dream. Orela had apparently been with the rest of the survivors, only venturing out when the group had heard the boys make their miraculous resurgence into the land of the semi-dry, nearly walking straight into the hole they had just escaped from in the process. Limping into the classroom, the boys found Leon and Jake waiting in the dark, looking confused and more than a little surprised in the thin flashlight beam. David slumped heavily into the chair at the teacher’s desk, arms braced, eyes locked on a far point in the floor that he wasn’t really seeing. Water still clung to him in rivulets, pooling at his feet as his clothes dripped a slow, steady rhythm. Orela crouched beside him, flashlight angled low as she tried gauging his pupils without blinding him further. "You’re gonna crash," she murmured. "Your system’s still in full burn. You need to rest." "Not yet," David muttered, not looking at her. "Don’t have time. I'll be fine." He wasn't fine. She could see that easily enough — the way he held his shoulder slightly wrong, the controlled quality of his breathing that meant he was managing something he wasn't acknowledging. He'd been in the water long enough and worked hard enough that the consequences were coming whether he cooperated or not. He knew it too. That was the problem. His heart was still hammering like it hadn’t realized the danger was over. His lungs ached, raw and tight. The skin over his back twitched with ghost-water, nerves refusing to settle. He could still feel the moment Dwight found him, how everything slowed, muffled, his thoughts collapsing inward. There hadn’t been enough air in the world. He refused to feel that again. But beneath the desk, his legs betrayed him, shaking faintly, despite how still he sat. His shoulder throbbed. Probably from ramming it into that desk in the stairwell. Or maybe from hauling Dwight by the arm like a sack of potatoes through a hallway that shouldn’t have existed. His spine pulsed with delayed adrenaline. Every second he didn’t move, he was losing ground. If he stopped pushing, stopped performing functional — the thing he'd been holding at arm's length since they'd clawed out of that hole was going to catch up with him. If he fell, he wasn’t sure he’d get back up. Orela sighed, casting the beam toward the door. The hallway stretched beyond it in flickering shadow, and for now, nothing stirred. Leon lingered near the door, glancing down the corridor with one hand on his empty holster. His shoulders twitched. There was a tightness in his movements — familiar tension, the darkness having set off a well worn in paranoia he couldn’t shake. Dwight had folded himself onto one of the low children's desks, shoulders slumped from the weight of the ordeal. His clothes were soaked, his face drawn. The adrenaline was draining fast, leaving him hollow and shaking. He looked vacant, but his hands gripped the edge of the desk tight, feet planted firm on the ground as if trying to anchor himself. He wasn't shaking anymore, not visibly, but the stillness had a quality to it that wasn't calm. His eyes tracked the room without settling on anything. Jake was perched on the counter, slamming the straight end of a half-rusted crowbar against the window. The glass refused to shatter, absorbing each strike with a soundless thud. He cursed under his breath and gave it a final smack before hopping off the counter. "This is insane. It's not even tempered glass. What the hell is this place MADE of?" David turned his head to face him. “How long have you three been up here, anyways?” “Been in here half an hour, maybe more,” Jake said, prying at the frame. “Thought it was just us and Orela. Doors started showing up everywhere and closed up behind us. Like the building didn’t want anyone else in. Feels like the place has doubled in size since we got in” Orela nodded in agreement, gesturing around the classroom with the flashlight. “Classrooms repeat. Some of them shift. I chalked it up to the usual Entity bullshit, but...” Dwight lifted his head slightly. “You guys got doors, we had faulty plumbing. Pipes were bursting. Something’s wrong with the space.” Leon’s brow furrowed. “Like... what?” “Distances felt off. Sounds vanished. Water rose faster than it should’ve. Way faster.” He swallowed. “It wasn’t just leaking. It was... flooding. Like it was pushing it through the floor. Way more than broken pipes should have had.” He kept his voice even and mostly managed it, though his hands tightened on the edge of the desk while he talked. "How fast?" Dwight hesitated. “Up to our ribs in minutes.” David grunted. “Hit the ceiling before we made it halfway down the connecting hallway.” He spared a glance at Dwight, who had gone back to curling against himself, voice soft. “It was so disorienting. Nothing was where it should have been. We lost my flashlight at some point... I had to go back to drag David out.” Leon nodded once, his hand clenched at his side, reflexive. A muscle twitched in his jaw. He looked down at the floor — to the thin spread of water that Dwight and David had tracked in with them, pooling dark against the tile — and he took one step to the side, away from the puddle he'd been standing in, without appearing to notice he'd done it. Jake looked around slowly, then back to the windows. “Weird that there’s five of us.” Orela blinked. “What?” Jake gestured vaguely with the butt of his crowbar. “There’s usually four, yeah? But with these two showing up together, that means it’s been five since the start.” "Trials run four survivors," he continued, looking around the group. "Four survivors, four generators, two gates. The whole thing's built around even numbers. So." He gestured vaguely at all of them. "Five." Nobody had a good answer for that. Dwight’s brows furrowed and he blinked slowly, the words catching something half-formed in his mind. He couldn’t quite place why, but something about it itched at him. Huffing lightly, he shook the feeling off. It was probably just the dark — the claustrophobia of it all. Orela had moved on to resume checking David's shoulder, unable to stay still in the silence anymore. David submitted to approximately four seconds of this before shifting away from her hands with an absent swat. "Stop it. I'm fine." "You're holding your arm like it's going to fall off." "It's not that bad. It’d feel better if you’d stop poking at it." Dwight watched the flashlight beam move around the room as Orela gestured, unwilling to lose track of the only light in the room. Every dip and bounce made his chest tighten. As she drifted around, fussing over an increasingly annoyed David, her steps disturbed the floor, making it ripple slightly. It took a moment to see it properly. Not floor. A film of water threading across the tiles. Dwight hissed and yanked his legs up on the desk before he'd finished processing what he'd seen — crouched, both hands white-knuckled on the edges — and the sound that came out of him was closer to a startled animal than a person. " No no nonono, David..." David turned, saw his face, followed his eyes. “Fuck...” He tried to stand, grip tight against the desk edge, only for his legs to fold like wet paper. Orela surged forward, catching him under one arm on reflex, nearly going down with him. He was heavier than he looked, all soaked muscle and bone and adrenaline backlash. "I've got it," He pulled his arm free, righting himself and stepping back from her, knees buckling slightly as he righted himself. “Said m’fine.” The water was there. A thin skin of it across the tile, barely a shimmer, running in from the hallway as quietly and patiently as everything else the building had done tonight. Dwight was already hunched in on himself, visibly shrinking from the puddle, a steady quiet stream of “not again” drifting on near hyperventilation as Leon rubbed small circles on his back. Panicking was not going to help things. “Hey. You’re okay. It’s not the basement. We can figure it out. We have time.” Dwight's knuckles were white on the desk edge, his breathing coming in shallow pulls that weren't quite keeping up with demand. His eyes had gone to the floor and stuck there, tracking the thin skin of water like it might lunge. "I know," he said. "I know, I just—" "I know," Leon kept his tone low, not following his gaze down. "We need to move." David's voice cut across the room, flat and certain. He was already looking at the door. "If it's still coming in, we don't have time to sit here." “Go where, exactly?” Jake snapped from the counter, "Windows won't break. I've been at this for twenty minutes. Whatever this glass is, it doesn't want to shatter. And we’ve struck out on the doors already." “Blocked like the stairs?” David asked. Jake and Leon shared a look. “Stairs?” “Ghostface blocked us in. Plugged up one of the stairwells with random crap. That’s why we had to go through the pipe hall. I think he’s still—” “Wait, he’s here?” Orela moved to hold David’s elbow again and only stepping back when he shot her a look full of steel and defiance. Dwight was trying to calm his breathing, to varying levels of success, redirecting his mind forcibly from the floor to literally anything else. “Didn’t you guys see him? He wasn’t even hiding when we came in. He was making a ton of noise." "We didn’t hear it," Jake looked down at the crowbar in his hand, thoughtful. "Actually, we've heard almost nothing this whole time. Building eats everything." Orela shook her head, confused. “There hasn’t been any kind of killer terror radius in here that we’ve felt. I had no idea he was even in this area. We had assumed whatever killer was assigned this trial got left outside.” “Besides,” Jake swung at the window one more time, crowbar bouncing harmlessly off, “The doors aren’t locked or blocked up. They’re jammed. The handles move fine, but the frame is swollen and warped so bad that the doors won’t budge.” Leon shared a meaningful glance with David and nodded. “That was when I was trying with Jake. With David, we have more muscle now. Between the three of us, we might be able to pry one of them open. What do you say? Feel up for a break and exit?” David looked at his shoulder. Rolled it once, deliberately. Took a couple steps, mentally logging the way his knees wobbled. The wince was small and controlled. He was steady enough for now. It would have to do. “Yeah. Ok. Let’s give it a go.” Orela swung her flashlight toward the hallway. The beam sliced the dark like a knife, catching on dust and soaked linoleum. “Let’s get out of here before the place decides we’re not interesting enough to keep.” In the hush that followed, Dwight kept his eyes on the floor. The water had reached the back wall. A thin layer, barely enough to splash — but moving. It was seeping in, quietly, purposefully. A slow reclaiming. Behind them, the walls pulsed. Just slightly. Jake glared at it with clear suspicion. The decision made itself, really. The front door had been the first thing Leon and Jake had tried and it was worth trying again with the full group behind it. Failing that, there were other exits. They'd work through them in order until something gave. The group filed out into the hallway, Orela's flashlight leading. Somewhere in the dark behind them, just outside the beam's reach, a shape kept pace. Danny tucked his phone into his sleeve and melted backward into the dark, footsteps silent despite the water — it had climbed past his ankles while he wasn't paying attention, which was mildly annoying, and his robes dragged through it with the heavy, sodden pull of fabric that had given up trying to stay dry. The long straps floated around him, trailing dark patterns across the surface. He'd have to do something about the mold smell later. The leather was going to hold it for weeks if he didn't treat it properly, and the canvas underlayer was probably already past saving if he was being honest with himself. Later problem. Right now, the beam of Orela's flashlight was painting the group in sharp relief — five people, wet and tired and moving with the grim purpose of survivors who had run out of other options — and he had a camera, a clear angle, and absolutely no intention of missing a single moment of what came next. He adjusted his position, keeping to the dark at the edge of the beam, and watched the rats work the maze. Ch 5 – Under Pressure The water lapped around their ankles with gentle, steady persistence. The hallway stretched longer than it had any right to as the group worked their way through, five shadows in single file, led only by the beam of Orela’s flashlight. The air hung heavy around them, thick with dampness and the sour rot of slow decay, clinging damp and thick to the inside of their throats. It felt unnatural. Processed. Rancid. Recycled through old pipes and bleeding walls. Every breath felt humid. Every movement whispered. The floor felt soft in places, like the linoleum had given up beneath the rising tide. The creeping flood found their calves before they'd made it halfway down the hall. Nobody announced it. Nobody needed to. It was just suddenly there, cool and present against skin that had almost — almost — dried out in the classroom, and the group absorbed the information in their own individual silences. Here we go again. That was the sum total of what Dwight's nervous system had to say about the situation, delivered with the flat certainty of something that had already been through this once tonight and had not enjoyed it. He kept his eyes forward and his breathing measured and his hands away from the walls because touching the walls meant feeling how damp they were, and feeling how damp they were meant thinking about where that moisture was coming from, and that was a thought he wasn't ready to finish. His footsteps stuttered through the water. Not enough to call attention, but enough to tell. His gaze kept flicking between the others, fingers twitching at his side. Five. That number had been pinging something at the back of his brain since Jake said it aloud. Five survivors. Five people. One too many. There was never supposed to be five. He couldn’t explain it, didn’t have the words for what it meant, but he felt it under his skin like a splinter. The Entity’s work was always symmetrical. Ritualistic. Four survivors. Four ways back to the campfire. Two exits. Balance was how the Fog functioned. Five was off. Five was bait. He didn’t see the water creeping higher anymore. Didn’t see the shadows moving differently. He saw numbers. Patterns. Ratios. He was spiraling inward like a whirlpool, understanding just barely out of reach. David limped alongside Dwight — jaw set, shoulders square, vision narrowed down to the hallway’s vanishing point. He was trying not to cough, breath kept shallow as he focused on the next few steps. If he kept his focus locked on the exit and ignored the pull of the water around his calves, maybe he wouldn’t feel how soft his knees had gotten. He desperately needed to rest. He could feel it behind his eyes, but he shelved it. Later. He could fold later. Once they were out. Leon kept his eyes on the middle distance. Not the floor. Definitely not the floor. Dwight’s warning about the water rising faster than natural echoed in his head like a drip. Ribs in minutes. Ceiling in under half an hour. He knew what that kind of pressure felt like, lungs too tight, world flipping upside down. He'd looked at the floor once, briefly, when the water was still just a shimmer across the tile back in the classroom, and something in the back of his brain had pulled up a memory he hadn't asked for — dark lake water, the specific pressure of something large moving beneath him — and he'd slammed the door on it before it could finish the sentence. He was fine. The hallway was flooded, not a lake. Completely different. He kept his eyes up. The memory knocked again, politely, and he ignored it. Jake hadn't stopped glaring at the walls since they left the classroom. Not the water, not the ceiling, not the general wrongness of the hallway — the walls specifically, like he was waiting to catch them doing something. His grip on the crowbar hadn't loosened since they'd left the classroom. “This whole building's rotting from the inside out, Entity’s in the fuckin’ plumbing,” he muttered. “Watch your backs. Wouldn’t be surprised if Her creepy-ass bug legs burst out of the floor next.” “Maybe don’t tempt her, huh?” Orela muttered softly, sweeping her light nervously around the edges where the water met the walls. "I'm just saying. She's right there. In the walls, in the pipes, in the floor. You can feel Her watching." "I know She's watching. That's exactly why you should stop—" " She’s been fucking with us from the start. I’m sick of being watched and lied to by a building. It's like She thinks we can't tell." Jake gestured broadly at the hallway around them, water sloshing at his calves. "This is insulting, honestly. She's not even—" "Jake." "—being creative about it, She's just—" Orela whipped around. “Can you fucking not?” Jake blinked. “What?” “I swear to every crawling god in this place, if you piss Her off more...” A crack split the wall to his left. Not fast. Not dramatic. Just a long slow fracture opening across the plaster from ceiling to baseboard, a deliberate and unhurried thing, trailing a thin seep of dark water from its edges like a signature. It bled down the wall and joined the water at their feet without ceremony. The hallway went very quiet, the crack pulsing once then settling. David turned away from the crack, his breath settling awkward and sharp in his chest. “Don’t think She appreciates you shit-talking Her.” Orela’s mouth was a tight line. “Maybe don’t provoke the possessed demon school until after we find a way out of it?” Jake gave a noncommittal grunt and turned back to the hall ahead, the flashlight finally landing on the warped shape of the front exit. The front door looked like it had been underwater for years. The wood had swollen into something barely recognizable — bloated and dark, the grain split in long weeping lines, the hinges reduced to rust suggestions that had long since fused to the frame. Mold trailing up the frame like veins. Metal and wood warped, paint bubbling in patches where water had soaked up from the base. Handles gleamed slickly. It looked less like a door now and more like something exhumed from the bottom of a lake. Leon ran his hand along the edge of the frame, checking the gap — or rather, checking for where the gap should logically have been. The seal was complete. "Still swollen shut. Could maybe force it, but..." He shook his head. "She’s got it tight." They crashed against it together, shoulders bruising, knuckles white around the warped handles. The frame groaned but didn’t give. The impact landed with that same swallowed quality that everything in this building had, sound dying before it could properly echo, the force going somewhere that wasn't even remotely useful. David bounced off the wood, water splashing against him as he staggered back, and something in his chest pulled wrong. He came away coughing — a hard, wet sound that had been building since the pipe hallway and had finally found its moment. "You alright?" Orela asked. "Fine," David rasped, waving her off as he fought back another wave. He rolled his shoulder, grit in his voice. "Just need a better angle." The next crash echoed flatly through the hall, but the doors didn’t move. Only the building seemed to groan louder, the heavily frosted glass of the windows flexing visibly in their frames. They tried again, straining, shoving, water slapping against their thighs with every surge, but the entryway held. Swollen. Bound. Denied. Nothing. Again. Still nothing. The hinges groaned in complaint. The crowbar idea was, theoretically, a good one. In practice, the door presented a significant obstacle to the theory — specifically, the complete absence of any gap to wedge the crowbar into. The seal was total, wood swollen flush against frame, and getting any kind of purchase meant chipping at the surface first. Wood flaked off in damp curls, but the door refused to budge. Leon jammed the tool into the edge, grunting with effort as he tried to lever the door free. David threw his weight in behind him, but the frame was a solid mass. No gap. No give. Leon braced with the crowbar again, gritting his teeth as he levered the swollen seam. David slammed his shoulder over and over, water splashing high with each hit. Orela tried to keep the light steady, her beam jerking with every shudder. The water had found their knees. David slammed his shoulder into the door again and had to pause against it, coughing, low and harsh, hand to his chest. Spitting out a mouthful of dark water, he resumed efforts again, trying to focus. Orela hovered nearby, eyes darting between the wall leak and David’s poorly masked pause. “This isn’t working. It’s not going to open,” she said softly. “We need to try the back exit.” His hands tightened on the crowbar. They had been at this door for — he didn't know how long. Long enough that his shoulder had moved from insistent to genuinely angry. Long enough that the small pile of waterlogged wood chips floating away from their feet represented real effort, real time, and he was not interested in walking away from it. "Just a little more," he said. "We're close." Dwight’s gaze darted down. The water was higher, having crept past his knees when he wasn’t paying attention. His breath hitched. He shook his head, words tumbling out too fast. "We’re wasting time. We have to move, try another exit. If we stay here..." He reached toward Orela’s flashlight, tugging at her sleeve as if to pull the beam with him. Panic edged his voice. "We have to go. Now." Leon braced harder against the lever, jaw set. "It’s just wood. It’ll give. I’ve broken worse. We stop now, it’ll open the second we walk away." His voice was calm, but iron. He wasn’t quitting. Not yet. “You guys are going to hurt yourselves like that! We need to try the other door!” David slammed his shoulder in again, wincing at the vibration through bone. "He’s right, we can’t stop. One more hit. Just one more." Orela looked between them — Dwight on one side with his hand on her arm, David and Leon on the other side still chipping at a door that had demonstrated absolutely no interest in cooperating — and felt the particular frustration of someone caught between two arguments that were both correct. They were going to hurt themselves if they kept going. They were also losing time standing here debating it. Both things were true and neither of them helped. "David—" "Not yet." “Guys we have to GO—" Her beam swung wildly, catching both of their faces in harsh slices of light. "Enough!" she barked, but it carried no decision, only the desperate need for one. Jake had been quiet through all of this. He'd stepped back from the door a minute ago, watching the group with an expression that had shifted from impatient to something more considered. "Hey." His voice cut through cleanly. "She wins if we keep doing this." Heads snapped towards him. "This." He gestured at the two of them at the door, at Dwight pulling at Orela, at the whole arrangement. "This is exactly what She wants. Us at each other’s throats. It doesn’t matter who’s right. If we keep arguing, we’re done.” David's hands had stilled on the crowbar. Leon had gone quiet. "We move," Jake said. "Together. Now." David and Leon stilled, leaning on the warped frame. Breathless, soaked, they staggered back, chests heaving. The tension in the air was palpable, both seeming to notice it properly for the first time. Leon looked to David. Waited. Another cough. A breath. David flexed lightly against the urge to argue. Jake was right, but that didn't make admitting defeat against a slab of rotten wood any easier. He gave the door an annoyed kick, water back-splashing against him in protest, then turned away from it. “Yeah. Ok. Let’s move.” Danny crouched low in a side room, the glow of his phone screen barely visible as he filmed their retreat, the survivors’ shapes bobbing in and out of the flashlight’s beam. From this angle, they looked less like people and more like fish in a tank, drifting through a hallway-turned-aquarium. Every splash, every stagger, every breathless mutter... it was art. He whispered into his mask, chuckling. "Swim faster, little minnows. Let’s see if you find the glass." Chapter 6 – Undertow The hallway had become a canal. Not dramatically — nothing in this building did anything dramatically anymore, preferring instead the slow patient version of every terrible thing. But somewhere between the front door and here the water had found the doorways and claimed them, rising until every opening along the hall was half-submerged, dark water lapping at the top of the frames with the quiet satisfaction of something that had been working toward this for a while. Orela kept the flashlight forward and her pace steady. The surface shimmered with movement, but the flashlight’s beam couldn’t break through it. Too murky. Too reflective. Orela swept the light ahead, but it bounced back off the water like a mirror. The floor beneath it was invisible, with nothing to mark where the hallway ended and the hazards began. Every step was a guess. Every footfall could find solid tile or find nothing, and there was no way to know which until weight was committed. “If you lose your footing in this,” Orela warned, “We won’t even see where you went down.” The water was too high now — licking mid-thigh — and the currents too deliberate. It tugged faintly, not downward, not outward. Away. From the walls. From the edges. Like the hallway itself was breathing inward. Jake squinted at the far end. “It’s pulling... do you feel that? It’s not just rising. It’s pulling...” Dwight pushed past him, pale and jittering, every nerve screaming at him not to stand still anymore. “One at a time. We stick to the wall.” They moved slowly. One of the basement stairwells appeared to their left — or rather, the top of its railing did, a few inches of metal standing above the waterline like a grave marker. Dwight glanced at it and quickly looked away. It shouldn’t have even been there in the first place, he noted mentally, not that it mattered. Nothing matched the layout he remembered anymore, and he would rather not think about it anyways. Orela led them forward, flashlight tucked high against her collarbone, her feet making slow steady slides across tile she couldn’t see. The beam caught glimpses of things beneath the surface — floating debris, a binder bloated with water, the shredded edge of a backpack. None of it sat still. The current nudged everything forward. The tiles were rough in places, near frictionless in others. She wished the light would break the surface better so at least she could tell what was in there. Her toes grazed a sharp edge, foot sliding suddenly into nothing, the tile vanishing beneath her. She jerked to a stop, hand flailing briefly for balance. Leon caught her arm on reflex, tugging her back from the edge. The light swung wildly, and the rest of the group froze in place behind her. Her flashlight beam skimmed across the water, catching the subtle fall where ripples slipped away into nothing. The hole into the basement was gone, swallowed entirely, leaving only a swirl of dark water that tugged on her legs expectantly. She stepped back quickly, steadying herself. “It’s open here,” she whispered. “Holy shit, I almost missed it completely.” David flinched lightly at the ripples. “Should have seen that coming. Let me guess. Swim across?” “We’re not backtracking,” Orela replied, voice firm. “I’m not going to risk wasting time checking classrooms to see if there’s a roundabout way past. This is... unpleasant, but more direct. If we keep a hand on the wall and take it slow, it’s not even that far across.” She didn’t wait for argument. Slid down into the water, slow and deliberate, then pushed off from the edge. Her body cut clean through the surface, shoulders rising above the pull, and with a few practiced strokes, she crossed the open gap. On the other side,
